newsitem.title: USA: Intel's upbeat forecast boosts stock.
newsitem.headline: Intel's upbeat forecast boosts stock.

text.p: Intel Corp. stock surged Tuesday on the computer chip giant's upbeat revenue forecast for the third quarter as investors tried to capitalise on evidence of a strengthening PC market.
Intel stock shot up $5.625 to $94.25 on Nasdaq, where it was the most actively traded stock with more than 19 million shares changing hands.
Many other semiconductor stocks rose on Intel's coattails. Atmel Corp. climbed $4.125 to $28.25, and Altera Corp. gained $4 to $52.125, both on Nasdaq.

Other gainers were LSI Logic Corp., which rose $1.25 to $23.25 on the New York Stock Exchange and S3 Corp., which gained $1.25 to $17.25 on Nasdaq. Applied Materials Inc., which makes chip fabrication equipment, rose $1.625 to $27.375 on Nasdaq.
The Philadelphia Stock Exchange's Semiconductor Index rose 8.79 points to 181.87 and the technology-driven Nasdaq composite hit 1,203.31, a 9.35-point increase.

Wall Street analysts said, however, that although Intel is the world's largest computer chip maker, the Santa Clara, Calif.-based company is not a mirror of the industry because of its unique position as a near-monopoly seller of microprocessors -- the heart of the personal computer.
"The situation at Intel is remarkably different than the rest of the industry," said analyst Drew Peck of Cowen & Co.

"Here you have a company that is a virtual monopoly in what is arguably the largest end market in the technology business -- selling microprocessors for PCs," Peck continued. "That gives them enviable control over the pricing environment. They can modulate their prices while the rest of the semiconductor industry is reeling from price erosion."

Peck and others said chip stocks were rallying because of Intel's revised forecast for a 5 percent increase in sales when it reports third-quarter earnings Oct. 14. The company in July had predicted that third-quarter sales would be flat with second quarter's $4.62 billion.

"There are a lot of different segments of the semiconductor market, and their dynamics differ," said Greg Mischou of Alex Brown. "Intel has a unique, differentiated product and they'll experience different conditions."
Still, a number of semiconductor makers which sell products to PC makers will benefit from strengthening PC sales, as Intel has, said John Lazlo of brokerage PaineWebber.
"It is not only very positive for Intel, it is supportive of other semiconductor makers" that have a sizeable PC market, like S3 Corp. or Atmel, Lazlo said.

But there is excess supply and manufacturing capacity of so-called commodity chips, such as memory chips, analysts said. That situation lowered memory chip prices to a fraction of what they fetched a year ago.
"Intel is immune to price erosion because they control prices," said Dataquest analyst Gary Grandbois.
In addition, markets for power transistors such as those made by Motorola Co. and International Rectifier Corp., and chips for analogue systems are all pretty weak, Grandbois said.
Micron Technology Inc. and Texas Instruments Inc. are the largest U.S. memory chip makers. Micron rose $1.125 to $26.75 and Texas Instruments climbed $1.75 to $50.375, both on the NYSE.
"We expect a slight rise in the industry over the rest of the year, but that is coming out from a trough," Grandbois said.

"There are pockets of weakness," including memory chips, he said. "We see a return to some small growth in the fourth quarter, but none of that is going to change the fact that it was a pretty poor year."
Intel, however, is expected to have a good fourth quarter. While the industry's sales are expected to drop by about 7 percent, Intel's are forecast to rise by double digits, analysts said.

Analysts Peck and Mischou said Intel has benefited from price drops bedevilling other semiconductor companies. Lower memory prices led PC makers to sell some products at lower prices, fuelling sales. In other cases, PC manufacturers chose to keep prices level but put in more advanced microprocessors, resulting in higher revenues for Intel.
"Intel cleans up" either way, Peck said.
